clinicalPearls: Paraneoplastic syndromes are disorders accompanying benign or malignant tumors that are NOT due to direct mass effect, invasion, or metastasis; neuroendocrine tumors such as small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) and carcinoids are especially common sources, and these syndromes are more common than generally appreciated (Harrison 22e p.736).

Hormones may be eutopic (from normal tissue of origin) or ectopic (atypical source); ectopic expression is often quantitative rather than absolute and is characterized by defective feedback regulation (e.g., ectopic ACTH) and release of large, unprocessed precursor peptides such as POMC (Harrison 22e p.736).

The three most common paraneoplastic endocrine syndromes are hypercalcemia from PTHrP overproduction, hyponatremia from excess vasopressin (SIADH), and Cushing's syndrome from ectopic ACTH (Harrison 22e p.737).

Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to 20% of cancer patients, is most often caused by PTHrP, and favoring features over primary hyperparathyroidism are known malignancy, recent onset, and very high calcium; PTH is suppressed and an elevated PTHrP is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcemic cancer patients (Harrison 22e p.737-738).

HHM produces hypercalciuria and hypophosphatemia like hyperparathyroidism, but is typically accompanied by metabolic alkalosis rather than the hyperchloremic acidosis of hyperparathyroidism; lymphomas can cause hypercalcemia via 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D rather than PTHrP (Harrison 22e p.737-738).

Ectopic vasopressin causes SIADH in at least half of SCLC patients; hyponatremia with low serum osmolality occurs alongside an inappropriately normal or high urine osmolality, and intake of free water (oral or IV) can rapidly worsen the hyponatremia (Harrison 22e p.738).

Ectopic ACTH accounts for 10-20% of Cushing's syndrome; SCLC is the leading cause, followed by bronchial and thymic carcinoids; plasma ACTH is usually >22 pmol/L (>100 pg/mL) and urine-free cortisol is typically more than 2-4 times normal (Harrison 22e p.738-739).

Ectopic ACTH Cushing's differs from pituitary disease: less weight gain/centripetal fat (brief exposure plus cachexia), but prominent fluid retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, glucose intolerance, and hyperpigmentation from MSH within the POMC precursor (Harrison 22e p.739).

Most ectopic ACTH sources fail to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone (8 mg suppresses ~80% of pituitary adenomas but fails in ~90% of ectopic cases), though bronchial and other carcinoids are notable exceptions that may show pituitary-like feedback (Harrison 22e p.739).

Non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia is driven by IGF-II precursor; serum IGF-II may not be markedly elevated, but an IGF-II/IGF-I ratio greater than 10:1 is suggestive, and the responsible tumor is usually large (>10 cm) and clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.739-740).

Oncogenic (tumor-induced) osteomalacia from FGF23 (phosphatonin) presents with low serum phosphorus, renal phosphate wasting, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, but NORMAL serum calcium and PTH; it is usually caused by benign mesenchymal tumors and reverses with tumor resection (Harrison 22e p.739-741).

Among paraneoplastic hematologic syndromes (erythrocytosis, granulocytosis, thrombocytosis, eosinophilia), red/white/platelet elevations are usually self-limited and asymptomatic; by far the most consequential hematologic abnormality in cancer patients is hypercoagulability (Harrison 22e p.740).

Migratory or recurrent thrombophlebitis can be the initial manifestation of cancer; peripheral venous thrombosis coexisting with visceral carcinoma, especially pancreatic cancer, is termed Trousseau's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.741).
harrison.pathophysiology: Neoplastic cells, particularly those of neuroendocrine origin (SCLC, carcinoids), secrete peptide hormones, cytokines, and growth factors or induce antibody production, altering endocrine, hematologic, and other systems independently of tumor bulk. Most ectopic hormone production reflects cellular dedifferentiation with derepression of developmental gene programs (epigenetic changes, altered microRNA expression); genetic rearrangements bringing a hormone gene under aberrant regulatory control are a rare alternative mechanism. HHM arises chiefly from tumor PTHrP, which binds the PTH receptor to mimic hyperparathyroidism (driven by PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli, TGF-beta, Ras activation, p53 loss); lymphomas may instead convert 25-OH vitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. SIADH results from ectopic vasopressin (often with co-expressed oxytocin) causing water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. Ectopic ACTH comes from unregulated POMC expression, with release of large biologically inactive fragments plus small amounts of active ACTH; very high cortisol overwhelms renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type II, allowing cortisol to act at mineralocorticoid receptors and produce severe hypokalemia. IGF-II precursor (from loss of 11p15 imprinting) causes hypoglycemia by acting on insulin/IGF-I receptors and suppressing GH and insulin. FGF23 forms a ternary complex with klotho and renal FGF receptors to reduce phosphate reabsorption and inhibit 1-alpha-hydroxylation. Hematologic syndromes are mediated by ectopic erythropoietin (erythrocytosis); G-CSF, GM-CSF, IL-6 (granulocytosis); IL-6/thrombopoietin (thrombocytosis); IL-5 (eosinophilia); and poorly defined procoagulants/cytokines (hypercoagulability).
additionalDifferentials: Non-malignant causes of SIADH: CNS trauma, infection, pulmonary disease, medications including many chemotherapeutic agents
Pituitary (Cushing's disease), adrenal adenoma, and iatrogenic/exogenous glucocorticoid causes of Cushing's syndrome
Polycythemia vera and hemoglobinopathies with increased O2 affinity (vs paraneoplastic erythrocytosis)
Renal, adrenal, or thyroid insufficiency as causes of hyponatremia
infectionMimics: Granulocytosis from infection or tumor necrosis mimicking paraneoplastic granulocytosis
Eosinophilia with pulmonary infiltrates resembling infectious or hypersensitivity pneumonitis
nonInfectiousMimics: Insulinoma or factitious hypoglycemia (vs IGF-II tumor hypoglycemia)
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium with PTH (suppressed in HHM) and PTHrP level; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in suspected lymphoma
Serum sodium and osmolality with paired urine osmolality and urine sodium for SIADH

Plasma ACTH, urine-free cortisol, high-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppression test, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation (>3:1 central:peripheral ACTH ratio suggests pituitary source)
Serum glucose with insulin, IGF-II, and IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1 suggestive) for tumor hypoglycemia
Serum phosphorus, FGF23, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D for oncogenic osteomalacia; octreotide scan to localize tumor
Hematocrit, red cell mass, and serum erythropoietin for erythrocytosis
Compression ultrasonography/impedance plethysmography (venography if equivocal) for DVT; ventilation-perfusion scan, chest radiograph, ECG, and ABG for suspected pulmonary embolism
Functional imaging (CT, MRI, PET, octreotide scintigraphy) to localize hormone-producing tumors, particularly when endocrine features precede cancer diagnosis
redFlags: Markedly elevated calcium (>3.5 mmol/L [>14 mg/dL]) with fatigue, altered mentation, polyuria, dehydration, or arrhythmias (short ST/QT, bundle branch block, bradyarrhythmia)
Severe hyponatremia (Na <115 meq/L) or any hyponatremia with confusion, depressed mental status, or seizures
Profound hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis and hypertension in ectopic ACTH; opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, mycoses) are a frequent cause of death
Increased venous thromboembolism risk in ectopic ACTH and in cancer generally; migratory/recurrent thrombophlebitis or clot in an unusual site
New atypical clinical or metabolic findings in a known cancer patient should prompt consideration of a paraneoplastic syndrome
Markedly elevated eosinophils (>5000/uL) causing dyspnea, wheezing, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates
harrison.prognosis: Endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes can cause substantial morbidity and may be the presenting clue to an occult malignancy; treatment of the underlying tumor is the mainstay but rarely alters overall survival or cancer progression. Hematologic cell-count syndromes are generally self-limited and asymptomatic, but thrombocytosis can mark advanced-stage disease and poorer prognosis. Hypercoagulability is the most consequential hematologic complication, and oncogenic osteomalacia and several endocrinopathies can reverse with successful tumor resection; checkpoint-inhibitor-associated endocrinopathies are generally irreversible and require lifelong hormone replacement.
pitfalls: Attributing atypical metabolic or neurologic findings to the malignancy or its treatment and overlooking a paraneoplastic syndrome
Confusing HHM with primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH should be suppressed and acid-base pattern differs (alkalosis in HHM vs hyperchloremic acidosis in hyperparathyroidism)
Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, which can precipitate central pontine myelinolysis; correction should be gradual (about 0.5-1 meq/L per hour)

Excluding ectopic ACTH on the basis of high-dose dexamethasone suppression alone, since bronchial/thymic carcinoids can suppress like pituitary adenomas; conversely a suppressed ACTH indicates an ACTH-independent cause
Relying on serum IGF-II levels, which may be normal in tumor hypoglycemia because assays may miss IGF-II precursors (use the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio)
Over-relying on D-dimer in cancer patients, where it is less predictive of DVT and rises with age without thrombosis

Pursuing extensive cancer work-up after a first unprovoked thrombophlebitis or PE in a patient without cancer; targeted evaluation is reserved for refractory, unusual-site, or migratory/recurrent clots
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal severity scale; severity is gauged by the magnitude and acuity of the biochemical derangement (e.g., calcium level and rate of rise, sodium level [Na <115 meq/L denotes severe hyponatremia], eosinophil count >5000/uL). For venous thromboembolism risk during chemotherapy, the Khorana risk score (Harrison Table 98-3) stratifies patients using cancer type, therapy, blood counts, and body mass index.
management: Direct definitive therapy at the underlying malignancy (commonly small-cell lung carcinoma or a carcinoid), as tumour control is the only measure that reliably corrects ectopic hormone secretion
Manage humoral hypercalcaemia with isotonic saline rehydration, an intravenous bisphosphonate or denosumab, and calcitonin for rapid short-term lowering
Treat ectopic-vasopressin SIADH with fluid restriction and, where needed, vasopressin-receptor antagonists, avoiding excess free-water intake that worsens the hyponatraemia
Control ectopic-ACTH Cushing's syndrome with steroidogenesis inhibitors such as ketoconazole or metyrapone, considering bilateral adrenalectomy for refractory hypercortisolaemia
Correct associated derangements such as IGF-II-mediated tumour hypoglycaemia and FGF23-mediated oncogenic osteomalacia, ideally by resecting the responsible tumour
Monitor serum calcium, sodium and cortisol during treatment as biochemical markers of tumour response and relapse
Coordinate care across oncology and endocrinology multidisciplinary teams
